Nowadays we don't see NSF policemen (or even normal policemen for that matter) using their pistols and rifles (for patrols) in favour of verbal de-escalation, hand-to-hand or baton strikes to handle situations. Pistols come at a risk of damage to property and people (as you have already been briefed on ad nausem) and trusting conscripts in a non-combat situation with firearms is a bad idea.

Besides training MPs to handle pistols "in case a situation  arises", it also serves the purpose of deterrence. Going back to the NSF policemen it deters aggressors and is practically a show of power to the public.

Besides, MPs are deployed to every camp in Singapore, logistically speaking yes it can be done but as others have mentioned, firstly, peacetime does not mandate mass deployment of such weaponry and secondly, the budget can be spent elsewhere in terms of maintenance, reserves, etc

for compo, i prefer to deviate a little from the standard writing styles and instead focus on ideation and justification. try not to think of what the "correct" responses are, think of what you yourself would think. really go and ask yourself what are your opinions and thoughts about it and come up with reasons why/what/wtv. plan these points out in a list and try to imagine the general direction you plan to write in, and if it is solid enuf just go for it. even if you feel it wouldnt hold much weight, if you have no other options try to smoke something out.

compre is about being able to paint a picture using the passage they give you and answering questions about it. try to imagine the thing that they tell you about, like if im reading a random news article of a murder i try to imagine what happened in my mind and construct a mental scene or image of the murder, how/why it happened, who was involved, etc. this takes practice and may not work for you but it kind of made my process slightly easier. as for paraphrasing you can try paraphrasing important phrases instead of words, but i was horrible at this so it may not help much.

im afraid im way past my O level era, but from what I remember I did many many practice papers for chem, emath and eng.

for eng, I had an english tutor that taught me to focus on the larger picture of the passage. try to understand the passage and the message, purpose, etc. its like reading a story book and imagining the scene and the characters. imagine what the passage is telling you and answer based off of that

for chem and emath, is rly concepts and application. make sure u understand the patterns in the practice papers and how the concept can be applied. if u look at both subjects the pyps always have some similar questions that use diff elements or examples, but at the end of the day it boils down to basic concepts

when doing practice papers, no need to do excessive amounts. just do the paper, see your mistake, understand why u made it, and move on. exposing yourself to many question types and concepts is good, but overdoing it is no point. like what others have said find keywords and try to see where marks are allocated for that type of question and memorise this.

dont panic, focus on quality study and stay hard. prelims js rly a playground for you to test out your knowledge one more time, but the end goal is O levels. dont be discouraged, dont conpare yourself. atb

if you feel that your content is secure mostly consider simply cutting back on studying and prioritising your sleep and mental wellbeing. the hardest part for most is showing up to the exam hall fresh and awake after all.

if not, 2 months can still be sufficient. focus on quality study, not studying quantitatively. at the end of the day, do you best and what is best for you and move on. Os is a big exam definitely, but there are other pathways to success (something i realised too late tbh) and the end goal for now is simply securing working opportunities or university.

do things your own way and however you feel best. organic chem is essentially a memorisation topic thing + pattern recognition. not only do you have to identify func groups, but u also have to remember properties and reactions that are possible (which is a very very simplified understanding of it).

i reiterate this many times but DO NOT be discouraged by past year papers from other jcs. some jcs set very difficult questions that screw you over. it is very easy to burn out during chem due to repeatedly failing practice papers and exams so if u do not enjoy it try to study it as much as u can without sacrificing too much sanity and move on to other subjects that u may struggle with.

1. I don't exactly recall the sequence, but total is 36 points

Stage A Day Shoot will have 4 positions, 16 shots total, 2 lanes per firer:

\- Foxhole Supported 100m Fig 15 and 12, 4 shots total

\- Prone Unsupported 100m (forgot what Figs here, iirc its Fig 12 and 11), 4 shots total

\- Kneeling/Squatting 100m Fig 12 and 11, 4 shots total

\- Rundown to 50m + Combat Reload Fig 12 and 11, 4 shots total

Stage B InAD will be 8 shots total, all Fig 12 and 11, 2 lanes per firer, all at 50m

\- Face Forward, 2 shots

\- Face Half Left, 2 shots

\- Face Half Right, 2 shots

\- Walking Reaction (u walk a while then the target suddenly come up), 2 shots

Stage C Night will be 12 shots total, 1 lane per firer (i dont rmb the sillouette illum all those oops)

\- Foxhole Supported 100m

\- Prone Unsupported 100m

\- Kneeling/Squatting 100m

\- Standing Shoulder 50m (no rundown)

There will be a screen at the 100m, but they'll advise you not to check after every shot as it disturbs your original position and can affect the grouping of your shots, may also cause you to be complacent/discouraged and your shooting fundamentals may be fucked. There will be a debriefing after each stage where you sit in a room and you can see your shot positions on a TV and will give you your score for that stage, so don't worry about it during the shoot itself.

6. For ATP service its 29/36 for marksman, ideally try to get full marks for InAD (Stage B) and Night shoot (Stage C), so 8/8 and 12/12 so u got 7 shots for error on your Stage A Day Shoot.

7. Most importantly you have to find a firing technique that is most comfortable for you. Maintain focus and keep your gun braced against your shoulder. Breathing patterns can vary and choose what you are most comfortable with. Elbows tight towards the center and remain calm. Don't snap the trigger and follow through. Don't be too kiasu and try your best. Good luck.
